summary: An older edition of the assigned numbers list, which records numbers used for networks and protocols. This RFC is historic. Replaced by RFC 870.

plainLanguage.summary: An old phone book of network numbers, kept because a newer edition replaced it.

subtitle: A registry of the numbers needed for Internet protocol implementations.

tldr.problem: Internet protocols use many assigned numbers (network addresses, protocol identifiers, port numbers, etc.). Without a central registry, confusion and conflicts would arise when multiple systems tried to use the same numbers.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 820 lists all assigned numbers from Internet protocols: network numbers in each class (A, B, C), version and protocol numbers for IP, TCP/UDP port numbers, Autonomous System numbers, and others. It serves as the single authoritative source.
tldr.outcome: Updated periodically as new protocols and assignments were needed. RFC 820 is Historic, replaced by RFC 870 and eventually by IANA registries. Modern assignment is managed through IANA (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority).

today: RFC 820 is Historic and has been obsoleted by RFC 870 and later registries. Modern assignment of protocol numbers, ports, and other Internet numbers is managed by IANA (the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority), which maintains living registries that are updated as new protocols are standardized.

sections.title: Introduction to Assigned Numbers
sections.content:
RFC 820 documents all the assigned numbers used in Internet protocol implementations. It is maintained by Jon Postel and represents agreement between DARPA and the network community about how numbers will be allocated to new protocols and systems.

The document is updated periodically. Whenever a new protocol is developed or a new system requires identification, the assignment is registered here. Before developing any protocol or application that needs a link, socket, port, protocol or network number, the protocol author should contact the IANA (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) for an assignment.

This RFC obsoletes earlier versions and documents the state of assignments as of January 1983.
sections.plainLanguage: This is like a master list of all the numbers that Internet protocols need. When someone creates a new protocol, they check this list to find an unused number and ask for it to be added.

sections.title: Network Numbers
sections.content:
The Internet Protocol (IP) uses 32-bit addresses divided into a network part and a local (host) address part. The division comes in three classes:

Class A networks use a 7-bit network number and 24-bit local address, with the high-order bit set to 0. This allows 128 Class A networks (though the first 10 bits constrain this further). Each Class A network can address 16 million hosts.

Class B networks use a 14-bit network number and 16-bit local address, with the first two bits set to 10. This allows 16,384 Class B networks, each with 65,536 addresses.

Class C networks use a 21-bit network number and 8-bit local address, with the first three bits set to 110. This allows over 2 million Class C networks, each with 256 addresses.

The RFC lists which networks have been assigned, their names, and the allocation category (R for Research, D for Defense, C for Commercial). Reserved addresses (like 0 and 127 in Class A, and 255 addresses in each class) are excluded from allocation.
sections.plainLanguage: Internet addresses are split into a network number and a local number, like a zip code and a street address. Three sizes were defined: Class A for big networks, Class B for medium, Class C for small. The RFC lists which ones were assigned to which organizations.

sections.title: Protocol Numbers and Ports
sections.content:
The Internet Protocol has fields for identifying the version (4 bits) and the next-level protocol (8 bits). The RFC assigns version numbers (version 4 for IP, version 5 for ST Datagram Mode, others reserved or unassigned) and protocol numbers.

Protocol numbers identify the transport or protocol layer above IP. For example, protocol 1 is ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol), protocol 6 is TCP (Transmission Control Protocol), and protocol 17 is UDP (User Datagram Protocol). The RFC lists all assigned protocol numbers and marks many as unassigned for future use.

In TCP and UDP, ports identify endpoints of logical connections. Well-known ports are assigned by the registry for standard services: port 21 for FTP control, port 23 for Telnet, port 25 for SMTP, port 53 for name servers, and many others. The RFC lists port assignments up to port 255, with the understanding that assigned ports have all but the low eight bits cleared to zero.
sections.plainLanguage: Each protocol packet includes a number saying which version it is and which protocol (like TCP or UDP) to use. Different services also have numbered ports to use, like 21 for file transfer and 25 for email. The RFC lists all these numbers.

sections.title: Autonomous Systems and Network Links
sections.content:
The Exterior Gateway Protocol (EGP) uses 16-bit numbers to identify Autonomous Systems (groups of gateways with a single routing policy). Only AS 1 is assigned in RFC 820 (to the BBN Gateways), with all others from 2 to 65,534 unassigned, allowing for future growth.

The original ARPANET used an 8-bit link field in the Host/IMP interface to identify packet types. Later this was extended to a 12-bit message ID, with the high 8 bits becoming the link number. Link numbers identify different protocol uses: link 0 for AHHP control messages, links 2-71 for regular AHHP messages, link 155 for Internet Protocol (regular), and others for experimental protocols and network maintenance.

Ethernet networks use a type field similar to ARPANET links. The RFC lists Ethernet type assignments for different protocol families: 2048 for IP, 1536 for Xerox NS IDP, 512 for Xerox PUP, and others.
sections.plainLanguage: Networks need numbers to identify themselves (AS numbers) and numbers to label different types of packets flowing through links. The RFC registers these numbers so networks can coordinate.
